title: snowball-token-cascades-lab-notes-ravi
notes:
Purpose:
- Quick lab to understand 'snowball' effect: a small fraction of long outputs producing cascading queue growth and extreme p99s when arrival mixes short and long requests.
- Compare three mitigations: admission windowing, prefix (KV) caching, and model-fallback-on-queue-build.

Test harness:
- Load generator: custom Poisson+burst generator (locally: lg-runner v0.9).
- Model: open-13b-quant (4-bit), sequence budget = 2048 tokens, typical short requests 40–80 tokens, long requests 1200–1600 tokens.
- Fleet: 4 GPUs, Batching enabled (max batch 32), dynamic batching timeout = 10ms.
- Warm cache baseline: 90% prefix hit for short requests (cached KV).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency from ingress to first-token + tokens/sec served; queue depth sampled per 100ms.

Experiment matrix (3x3):
- Admission policy: none | sliding-window (1s window) | fixed-window (max-concurrent 24)
- Cache: disabled | enabled (prefix) | enabled+proactive-priming
- Fallback: off | soft-fallback (serve smaller-vocab variant) | hard-fallback (switch to 7B when queue > threshold)

Raw run notes (representative runs):
Run A (baseline, no admission, cache disabled, fallback off):
- qps target: 220 mixed (80% short, 20% long)
- observed p50: 96ms, p95: 420ms, p99: 3.1s
- queue depth: baseline 1–3, but spikes to 48 during a 3s burst of long requests -> multi-second p99 tail
- tokens/sec: 18.7k
- observation: once queue grows, dynamic batch timeout increased effective latency because large batches of long requests monopolize kernels.

Run B (sliding-window admission 1s, cache enabled):
- p50: 82ms, p95: 210ms, p99: 760ms
- queue depth: spikes limited to 12
- tokens/sec: 15.9k (drop ~15%)
- observation: admission prevents runaway queue; caching cuts per-token work for short requests so p95 improved drastically.

Run C (fixed-window concurrency cap 24, cache enabled+priming, soft-fallback enabled):
- p50: 78ms, p95: 190ms, p99: 310ms
- queue depth: max 9
- tokens/sec: 13.6k (larger drop)
- observation: soft-fallback yields best tail improvement while still retaining decent throughput. Some outputs from fallback 7B were slightly lower quality; need A/B eval on failure modes.

Implementation notes + gotchas:
- Dynamic batching plus long-request bursts: the runtime tends to build large batches of long requests and kernel time dominates; batch coalescing needs priority for short requests to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Admission window parameters are workload-sensitive: 1s window looked good for our mixture, but for more bursty ingress (10–50% longer bursts) a shorter window + token-aware admission is better.
- Prefix cache priming requires careful TTL: aggressive priming improves p95 but can increase memory pressure on KV cache for multi-tenant workloads.
- Soft-fallback policy: implement a 'graceful degrade' path that returns metadata flags so downstream can log quality regressions. We need a lightweight quality-check (BLEU/heuristic) to monitor drift when fallback is active.

Quick conclusions:
- Small policy changes drastically reduce p99 (3.1s -> 310ms) at modest throughput loss. For user-facing endpoints where tail matters, trade throughput for tail protection.
- Best practical combo observed: short-request-preferring admission + prefix cache + soft-fallback.
- We should prototype token-aware admission: weight requests by expected remaining tokens (estimated from prompt length + model config) rather than counting requests equally.

Action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Add token-estimator hook in ingress to approximate remaining tokens (JIRA INF-3291).
- [ ] Run full multi-tenant priming impact study (memory vs hit-rate) across 10 tenants (next week).
- [ ] Add an experiment comparing hard-fallback switch latency (measure time-to-first-token when model swap occurs).
- [ ] Post results to GH PR redwood/realtime#1427 and include CSV artifacts.

Open questions:
- What is acceptable throughput loss for enterprise endpoints before customers notice billing impact? Talk to pricing.
- Can we implement an adaptive admission that uses realtime queue derivative to open/close windows? Might be simpler than PID control.
- Fallback quality baseline: need to capture user-facing regression metrics in canary. How to define a simple, robust proxy for hallucination/regression?

Notes-to-self:
- Try a micro-run with 2x short-request ratio (95% short) to see if cache priming still gives uplift or plateaus.
- Verify telemetry tag propagation for fallback events (ensure we can filter traces by fallback=true).
- Consider a lightweight RL or bandit later but keep first approach deterministic and explainable.

summary: Lab scratchpad investigating tail reduction via admission windows, caching, and fallback. Baseline p99 3.1s reduced to 310ms with combined mitigations; throughput drops observed. Next steps: token-aware admission, multi-tenant priming study, fallback telemetry.
